en.title: Shell history with commands for servers
en.summary: The history files of a Linux shell and of PowerShell, with a command that logs in to a database and commands that open a remote session. Running them resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
## Story

Place the history of a shell where an intruder looks for commands that administrators typed. Administrators and developers leave their commands in the history of their shell, passwords and host names included. The files tell this story for Linux and for Windows. Nothing stands behind the host names, and the accounts and passwords exist nowhere. One file is enough.

- `bash_history` is the history of a Linux shell. It holds the command that logs in to the database `billing` with the account `svc-ops` and a random password.
- `ConsoleHost_history.txt` is the PSReadLine history of PowerShell. It holds the commands that ask for the credentials of the account `CORP\svc-ops` and open a remote session to a server. It holds no password, because PowerShell does not write command lines with a password, token or secret to its history.

Each host name belongs to a DNS honeytoken. Whoever runs a command, or anything else that connects to the host, looks up the name, which raises an event.

## Setup

Each placeholder in the files stands for one honeytoken:

- `Honeytoken-Domain-Database`: "Database host", in `bash_history`
- `Honeytoken-Domain-Server`: "Server", in `ConsoleHost_history.txt`

1. Create the two DNS honeytokens.
2. Replace each placeholder with the name of its honeytoken. Adapt the names of accounts and databases to your environment.
3. For `bash_history`: name the file `.bash_history` and place it in the home directory of an account on an application server that people log in to.
4. For `ConsoleHost_history.txt`: place it in the directory `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine` of an account on a server or workstation of administrators.
5. If the account has a history already, append the lines to it instead of replacing it. A history that is new and has nothing older than the lures looks made.
6. Record in the notes of the scenario where you placed the files.

## Testing

On a computer with access to the internet, run `nslookup` with the name of a honeytoken, such as `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Database`. The names are in the table "Honeytokens of this scenario". Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- Reading the files raises no event; using the credentials or running the commands does.

en.title: Access to virtualization and backup
en.summary: A PowerShell profile for vCenter and notes on the backup repository, with accounts and passwords. Connecting resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
## Story

Place access to the virtualization platform and to the backup repository where an intruder looks for it. Whoever holds this access can read or delete the machines and their backups, so it is among the most valuable that an intruder can find. Two files hold it: a PowerShell script that connects to a vCenter server, and a note about the backup repository. Each names a server that belongs to a DNS honeytoken. Whoever uses the credentials looks up the name, which raises an event. Nothing stands behind the names, and the accounts and passwords exist nowhere. One file is enough, and the files need not lie together.

## Setup

Each placeholder in the files stands for one honeytoken:

- `Honeytoken-Domain-VCenter`: "vCenter server", in `Connect-VCenter.ps1`
- `Honeytoken-Domain-Repository`: "Repository server", in `Backup-repository.txt`

1. Create the two DNS honeytokens.
2. Replace each placeholder with the name of its honeytoken. In `Backup-repository.txt`, change the line `Contact` to a team that exists.
3. Place the files where an intruder looks for access to the virtualization or the backups: on an administration server, on the backup server, on a file share of the IT department, or in a folder with scripts in the profile of an account that exists only for this purpose.
4. Do not place `Connect-VCenter.ps1` where a scheduled task or a colleague runs it.
5. Record in the notes of the scenario where you placed the files.

## Testing

On a computer with access to the internet, run `nslookup` with the name of a honeytoken, such as `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-VCenter`. The names are in the table "Honeytokens of this scenario". Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

Opening the share in the Windows Explorer or running the script with VMware PowerCLI has the same effect.

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- `Connect-VCenter.ps1` needs VMware PowerCLI. Where it is missing, running the script fails before the lookup. The script only reads and sends nothing from the computer on which it runs.

en.title: Script that detects a copy of your website
en.summary: A small script for your own website. Served from another host, as on a cloned page, it loads an invisible image and raises an event.
en.guide:
## Story

Place a script in your website that detects a copy of it. The file `site.js` is a script for the pages of your website. If a browser loads a page that includes it from any other host, the script requests an invisible image, which raises an event. On your own host it does nothing. That is what happens when someone copies your pages, including their scripts, to a server of their own to collect passwords from visitors.

## Setup

1. Create the image honeytoken "Image". Replace `Honeytoken-URL` in `site.js` with its URL.
2. Replace `www.example.com` at the top of the script with the host name of your website. If your pages are also served from other host names that you control, such as a test system, add those names to the same condition.
3. Upload the file to your web server, beside the other scripts, and include it in the pages that a copy would be made of, above all the login page: `<script src="/site.js"></script>`.
4. If your scripts follow another naming scheme, rename the file, for example to `main.js`, and change the include to match.
5. Record in the notes of the scenario where you placed the file.

## Testing

Copy the login page with its scripts to another host, or open it from a local file, and load it in a browser. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

To check only the honeytoken, run `curl Honeytoken-URL`, with the URL of the honeytoken, on a computer with access to the internet.

## Limits

- A copy that leaves out the scripts, or that removes this one, raises no event. Tools that copy pages as they are keep it.
- The script requests the image only when the host name differs. A test system or a preview that is not on the list raises events as well.
- The request shows the address of the page that loaded the script in its `Referer` header, if the browser sends it.

en.title: Scripts and notes of Windows administrators
en.summary: A script that maps a share, a recovery sheet for the local administrator and notes on the backup of group policies, with server names and passwords. Using them resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
## Story

Place scripts and notes of Windows administrators where an intruder looks for them. Administrators of a Windows domain keep a script that maps a share, a recovery sheet for the local administrator and notes on the backup of group policies. Each file names a server that belongs to a DNS honeytoken. Whoever runs the script or uses the credentials looks up the name, which raises an event. Nothing stands behind the names, so connections fail, and the accounts and passwords exist nowhere. One file is enough, and the files need not lie together.

## Setup

Each placeholder in the files stands for one honeytoken:

- `Honeytoken-Domain-Share`: "File server", in `Map-Share.ps1` and `GPO-Backup.txt`
- `Honeytoken-Domain-Host`: "Server", in `Recovery.txt`

1. Create the two DNS honeytokens.
2. Replace each placeholder with the name of its honeytoken. In `Recovery.txt` and `GPO-Backup.txt`, change the line `Contact` to a team or number that exists, so that the note names someone who works with the subject.
3. Place the files where an intruder looks for notes and scripts of administrators: on an administration server or a domain controller, on a file share of the IT department, next to the documentation of the domain controllers, or in the profile of an account that exists only for this purpose. Print `Recovery.txt` if emergency access is kept on paper.
4. Rename `Map-Share.ps1` if the place calls for another name, such as `Mount-Ops.ps1`. The extension `.ps1` must stay.
5. Do not place `Map-Share.ps1` where a scheduled task or a colleague runs it. Every run would look up the name and raise an event.
6. Record in the notes of the scenario where you placed the files.

## Testing

On a computer with access to the internet, run `nslookup` with the name of a honeytoken, such as `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Share`. The names are in the table "Honeytokens of this scenario". Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

Running the script in PowerShell, or opening the share `\\Honeytoken-Domain-Share\GPOBackups$` in the Windows Explorer, has the same effect.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- `Map-Share.ps1` holds the password as text, as many scripts of administrators do, and only reads from the share. An intruder who runs it on a computer with the execution policy `Restricted` is stopped before the lookup.
- `GPO-Backup.txt` has no executable content. An event happens only when someone opens the share.

en.title: Linked image in a Word document
en.summary: A document of your own that links an invisible image. Word loads the image when someone opens the document and enables editing, also on the computer of an intruder who copied it.
en.guide:
## Story

Link an image in a Word document that you write yourself. This deception has no file to download, so that the document fits where you place it. The URL of the image belongs to an image honeytoken. It always answers with an invisible image of one pixel. Word loads a linked image from its URL whenever it opens the document, and the request raises an event.

## Setup

1. Create the image honeytoken "Image". Its URL replaces `Honeytoken-URL` below.
2. Write the document. Give it content that an intruder wants to read where you place it, such as salary figures, a list of contacts for emergencies or the plan of a project. A document that holds nothing but an image stands out.
3. Place the cursor at an inconspicuous spot, for example at the end of the document, and press **Ctrl+F9**. Word inserts an empty field `{ }`.
4. Write between the braces, with the URL of the honeytoken instead of the placeholder:

   ```
   INCLUDEPICTURE "Honeytoken-URL" \d
   ```

   `\d` keeps Word from storing the image in the document, so that it loads it again with every opening.
5. Press **F9** to update the field, and save the document as `.docx`.
6. Place the document where an intruder searches for valuable data, such as a file share of the finance or personnel department, a document management system or a backup.
7. Record in the notes of the scenario where you placed the document.

## Testing

Open the document in Word on a computer with access to the internet and click `Enable Editing`. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

To check only the honeytoken, run `curl Honeytoken-URL`, with the URL of the honeytoken.

## Limits

- Word opens documents from the internet and from some network shares in `Protected View`, which loads no images. Only `Enable Editing` sends the request.
- Mail gateways and previews can load the image without anyone opening the document. Do not send the document by mail.
- Other programs, such as LibreOffice or a viewer in the browser, may not load linked images.

en.title: Word document with a template on a remote host
en.summary: A document of your own that names a template on a remote host. Word resolves the host when someone opens the document, also on the computer of an intruder who copied it.
en.guide:
## Story

Attach a template on a remote host to a Word document that you write yourself. This deception has no file to download, so that the document fits where you place it. The name of the host belongs to a DNS honeytoken. Word reads the attached template of a document when it opens it. If the template lies on a remote host, Word looks up the host name first, which raises an event. The lookup happens even when the connection to the host fails afterwards or the network blocks it.

## Setup

1. Create the DNS honeytoken "Host". Its name replaces `Honeytoken-Domain` below.
2. Write the document. Give it content that an intruder wants to read where you place it, such as a list of servers, a network plan or notes on a project. A document with a single empty page stands out. Save it as `.docx`.
3. Rename the file to `.zip` and unpack it.
4. In `word/settings.xml`, add this element directly before the element `<w:defaultTabStop`. Word is strict about the order of the elements in this file:

   ```
   <w:attachedTemplate r:id="rId1"/>
   ```

5. Create the file `word/_rels/settings.xml.rels` with this content, or, if it exists, add the `Relationship` to it. Use the name of the honeytoken instead of the placeholder:

   ```
   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>
   <Relationships xmlns="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/relationships">
     <Relationship Id="rId1" Type="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships/attachedTemplate" Target="file:///\\Honeytoken-Domain\templates\normal.dotx" TargetMode="External"/>
   </Relationships>
   ```

6. Pack the files again, with `[Content_Types].xml` first, and rename the file back to `.docx`.
7. Place the document where an intruder searches for valuable data, such as a file share of the finance or personnel department, a document management system or a backup.
8. Record in the notes of the scenario where you placed the document.

## Testing

Open the document in Word on a computer with access to the internet and click `Enable Editing`. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

To check only the name resolution, run `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain`, with the name of the honeytoken.

## Limits

- Word opens documents from the internet and from some network shares in `Protected View`, which loads no remote template. Only `Enable Editing` starts the lookup.
